item.title: Government breaks silence, confirms influenza activity increasing across Fiji
item.description: The Ministry of Health and Medical Services is urging Fijians to take precautions following a marked increase in influenza-like illnesses and acute respiratory infections across the country. Health surveillance has recorded a rise in cases over the past three weeks, while laboratory testing has confirmed increased seasonal influenza activity.
item.content:encoded:
The Ministry of Health and Medical Services is urging Fijians to take precautions following a marked increase in influenza-like illnesses and acute respiratory infections across the country.

Health surveillance has recorded a rise in cases over the past three weeks, while laboratory testing has confirmed increased seasonal influenza activity.

The Ministry is advising people who are sick to stay home and avoid spreading the virus to others.

Members of the public are also encouraged to cover coughs and sneezes.

Wash hands regularly with soap and water or use hand sanitiser.

Common influenza symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, body aches, headache, fatigue and a runny nose.

The Ministry is advising people to seek immediate medical attention if they experience difficulty breathing, chest pain or heaviness, confusion, severe vomiting or other concerning symptoms.

Health authorities said influenza activity would continue to be monitored and urged Fijians to take simple precautions to protect themselves, their families and the wider community.

item.title: Nine women unite to fight illegal dumping
item.description: A SIXTY-FIVE-year-old resident of Wailea St, Vatuwaqa has taken a stand against illegal rubbish dumping, volunteering with Trashboom Pacific to educate residents and help keep the community clean. Lavenia Volaukitoga said a group of nine women had been working together to discourage residents from dumping rubbish in the creek and surrounding areas.
item.content:encoded:
A SIXTY-FIVE-year-old resident of Wailea St, Vatuwaqa has taken a stand against illegal rubbish dumping, volunteering with Trashboom Pacific to educate residents and help keep the community clean.

Lavenia Volaukitoga said a group of nine women had been working together to discourage residents from dumping rubbish in the creek and surrounding areas.

“Our group has nine women, and we try and educate the residents here not to throw rubbish around or in the creek,” she said.

The group also photographs people dumping rubbish and sends the evidence to Trashboom Pacific for further action.

Ms Volaukitoga said a recent sewer line leak prevented Trashboom Pacific workers from accessing the trashboom and removing accumulated waste.

“Because of the sewer line leak, workers from Trashboom Pacific were not able to pick the rubbish and clean the trashboom.”

She said workers had resumed cleaning the trashboom, but she was saddened by what they were finding.

“The waste includes plastic bottles, cans, kitchen waste, diapers, household rubbish and dangerous items such as needles.

“I just wonder why people can’t throw them in waste bins provided by the council?”

Ms Volaukitoga welcomed the $200 spot fine for littering and hoped it would deter offenders.

“I am so happy that the $200 spot fine has been put in place and I hope this will solve this rubbish problem.

“I feel sorry for the workers from Trashboom Pacific who are going into the creek to pick up rubbish thrown by some irresponsible people of this community.”

item.content:encoded:
NEARLY 80kg of rubbish was hauled from the Wailea St trashboom in Vatuwaqa, Suva by the second day of cleaning yesterday, highlighting the scale of irresponsible dumping, with more than 30kg of diapers, 29kg of PET bottles and plastics, and potentially dangerous waste including used needles among the debris.

Trashboom Pacific environment data officer Bernadette Thomasina said the scale and nature of the waste highlighted the urgent need for people to change their attitude towards rubbish disposal.

“We’ve already collected more than 79kg of trash from this trashboom,” she said.

She said workers had collected about 30 bags of PET bottles in a single day, along with syringes.

“We also collected a bottle full of syringes yesterday. Today, just in 10 minutes, we found six syringes.”

She said workers had to proceed slowly and carefully because they were working in contaminated water.

“We are risking the lives of our workers because they go in a pool of contaminated water.”

Ms Thomasina said recyclable materials were separated and sent for recycling, while other waste was disposed of appropriately.

“The mentality of our fellow Fijians has to change if we want to see a change in our environment.

“You can’t be just throwing your trash anywhere you like.”

She urged people to consider the environmental and health consequences of careless dumping.

“Remember, what we throw into the sea, is what we eat.”

Ms Thomasina also reminded residents that those caught dumping rubbish irresponsibly face a $200 spot fine.

item.title: ‘Report may go public’ | PM Rabuka says Cabinet will consider it first
item.description: THE Constitution Review Commission’s report containing recommendations for Fiji’s new constitution could be made public after it is considered by Cabinet, Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says, as calls grow for its release. Speaking to the media yesterday, Mr Rabuka said Cabinet would receive the report first, allowing ministers time to study its contents before Parliament resumes later this month.
item.content:encoded:
THE Constitution Review Commission’s report containing recommendations for Fiji’s new constitution could be made public after it is considered by Cabinet, Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says, as calls grow for its release.

Speaking to the media yesterday, Mr Rabuka said Cabinet would receive the report first, allowing ministers time to study its contents before Parliament resumes later this month.

Asked whether the report would subsequently be released, Mr Rabuka said it could be made available electronically, likely online, allowing Fijians to access its contents without having to obtain what he described as a “voluminous book”.

He said Government would not select individual recommendations from the review, but would consider the views gathered through the commission’s public and stakeholder consultations as a whole.

The recommendations would first be considered by Cabinet before any proposed constitutional amendments were drafted into a Bill and taken to Parliament.

Mr Rabuka also called for calm following concerns raised in Facebook posts about issues contained in the report, saying such discussions could result in people taking hardline positions before the recommendations had been properly considered.

He also rejected suggestions that Fiji’s decision not to attend the Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ meeting in Palau was influenced by China.

Mr Rabuka said he had remained in Fiji to attend the presentation of the report to the President and that it would have been improper for him to be absent.

“We have not been influenced by anybody,” he said.

Meanwhile, Opposition MP Premila Kumar called on Government to immediately release the commission’s original report before making any changes to its recommendations.

Mrs Kumar said the constitutional reform process must be transparent and open to public scrutiny, arguing that Fijians could not meaningfully participate in the process without access to the documents.

item.title: Kayzia takes the stage
item.description: For Kayzia, this Saturday’s VT1S concert will be the biggest stage she’s ever been on. She’ll be performing three songs live for the first time.
item.content:encoded:
For Kayzia, this Saturday’s VT1S concert will be the biggest stage she’s ever been on.

She’ll be performing three songs live for the first time.

“For me, it’s a big thing because it’s my first time performing on stage,” she said.

“And the only time I’ve been singing was in church. So, this is going to be my first time performing my three songs on stage.”

She’s feeling both nervous and excitement as rehearsals ramp up with her team.

“I’m feeling nervous and excited too. Just practising, doing rehearsals.”

For Kayzia, going from singing in church to a festival crowd is a huge step.

She’s inviting everyone to come support and experience it with her.

item.title: BSP announces major leadership restructure in Fiji
item.description: BSP Financial Group has announced a major leadership restructuring aimed at strengthening its regional operations and succession planning. Michael Nacola, who has served as the Managing Director of BSP Life in Fiji for the past seven years, will step into the newly created role of Deputy Country Head for BSP Fiji.
item.content:encoded:
BSP Financial Group has announced a major leadership restructuring aimed at strengthening its regional operations and succession planning.

Michael Nacola, who has served as the Managing Director of BSP Life in Fiji for the past seven years, will step into the newly created role of Deputy Country Head for BSP Fiji.

He will report directly to BSP Fiji Country Head, Haroon Ali.

Mr Nacola will officially assume his new responsibilities once a successor is appointed at BSP Life.

A comprehensive internal and external search is currently underway to fill his vacant position.

In tandem with this appointment, Maikash Ali’s leadership portfolio has been expanded.

In addition to his current duties as Head of Corporate and Institutional Banking for Fiji, he has been promoted to Regional Head of Corporate and Institutional Banking.

item.title: Family members urged to share RHD burden
item.description: Caring for children living with rheumatic heart disease should not be a burden carried by mothers alone, says Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran. She made the comment while launching World Heart Month 2026 at the Grand Pacific Hotel as part of a global campaign to raise awareness on cardiovascular disease.
item.content:encoded:
Caring for children living with rheumatic heart disease should not be a burden carried by mothers alone, says Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran.

She made the comment while launching World Heart Month 2026 at the Grand Pacific Hotel as part of a global campaign to raise awareness on cardiovascular disease.

“Fathers, grandparents, guardians and extended family members all have a critical role to play in lifting this burden,” she said.

Ms Kiran urged parents and caregivers to take symptoms such as persistent sore throats and painful joints seriously and seek medical attention early.

She also called on people to regularly check their blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol to reduce the risk of heart disease and stroke.

“Every heartbeat matters. Each of us has a profound responsibility to protect our own health and the health of those we care for.”

Ms Kiran said financial hardship, transport difficulties, poor housing and limited access to services could prevent families from maintaining treatment.

The theme for World Heart Month 2026 is “Don’t miss a beat”.

item.title: Reconciliation identifies 61 cases for investigation
item.description: A TOTAL of 61 online-safety cases have been referred to the authorities for investigation, prompting the Online Safety Commission and police to strengthen the way serious complaints are tracked and progressed. Online Safety Commissioner Filipe Batiwale said victims needed greater certainty about their cases after they were referred for criminal investigation.
item.content:encoded:
A TOTAL of 61 online-safety cases have been referred to the authorities for investigation, prompting the Online Safety Commission and police to strengthen the way serious complaints are tracked and progressed.

Online Safety Commissioner Filipe Batiwale said victims needed greater certainty about their cases after they were referred for criminal investigation.

A recent reconciliation exercise between the two agencies identified 61 cases referred by the commission to the police.

Mr Batiwale said the two departments were working to improve the acknowledgement, tracking and progression of referrals and the sharing of case-status information.

“When someone comes to us, tells us what has happened, provides the material and goes through the complaint process, they understandably want to know what happens next,” he said.

“If we refer that matter for criminal investigation, OSC and police both need a clear system that allows the case to be tracked and, where appropriate, allows the complainant to be told where things stand.”

He said the issue was not about blaming either institution, but ensuring their respective roles worked effectively together.

“Police have a very large mandate. They deal with every type of crime in Fiji. OSC has a specialist mandate.

“We need to make sure those two roles work together properly instead of creating unnecessary duplication.”

Mr Batiwale said serious online complaints could involve children, intimate images, threats, exploitation, fake accounts and digital evidence that could disappear quickly.
